items.source_type: intergovernmental composite index plus independent national statistical survey
items.evidence_location: WIPO GII 2026 landing page, top-10 rank and country profile; WIPO GII 2024/2025 rank; NCSES BERD 2024 Table 1 and survey-description section.
items.specific_finding: The United States ranks 3rd in WIPO GII 2026 (also 3rd in 2024 and 2025), while its independently measured business R&D rose to US$765.1bn in 2024 (+6.0% from 2023). This supports a durable high-investment innovation system, not an improving overall GII rank.
items.primary_evidence_summary: WIPO 2026 lists Switzerland 1st, Sweden 2nd and USA 3rd. NCSES/Census BERD survey records $765.082bn US domestic business R&D in 2024 versus $721.792bn in 2023; own-funded share was about $679bn. Separate NCSES 2026 State of US S&E overview reports businesses performed 77% of estimated national R&D in 2024.
items.corroboration_assessment: NCSES is independent of WIPO and uses actual US enterprise-survey spending rather than composite country ranks; it corroborates the scale and business orientation, not WIPO’s ranking methodology. WIPO 2025 verifies that overall rank did not improve.
items.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Large commercial R&D investment and deep private-sector financing create industrial translation capacity; the GII composite captures multiple system pillars but cannot establish causation or single-technology superiority.
items.eu_radar_comparison: Not identified in the supplied main Radar. Adds independently measured innovation-system context, correcting any narrative that 2026 represents a US upward move in overall GII placement.
items.method_and_limitations: Composite rank sensitive to definitions, missing data and changing indicators; year-to-year ordinal rank is not causal. 2024 business R&D is historical data released October 2026, not 2026 R&D spending, and US dollars are nominal.
items.reviewer_notes: 2024 and 2025 WIPO rank also third. Do not mistake the 2024 reference year for a 2026 spending amount.

items.source_type: Independent think-tank policy analysis / structural technology-market evidence
items.evidence_location: ECFR sections “China leads on AC,” “Saying no to adaptation,” and “What Europeans should do”; International Energy Agency (IEA), 10 July 2026, sections “More air conditioners are being sold” and Chinese manufacturing capacity.
items.specific_finding: China’s large-scale cooling-equipment manufacturing and supply chains are a strategically relevant technological capability for adaptation to rising heat demand: IEA estimates roughly 170 million Chinese AC units manufactured and 60 million exported per year, while ECFR documents the resulting European sourcing dependencies and Chinese firms’ product localisation.

items.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Cooling is becoming essential energy infrastructure; supply concentration shapes access to efficient appliances, adaptation technology, product standards and research-to-manufacturing scale-up. European resilience depends on efficiency innovation, diversified supply chains and careful technology-transfer choices.
items.eu_radar_comparison: The exact ECFR commentary is already in the main Radar. This verification extends it with IEA’s independent manufacturing and electricity-demand data, and reframes it as structural innovation and industrial capability rather than evidence of a new laboratory breakthrough.

items.verified_title: India converts selected innovation capabilities into outputs despite constrained R&D intensity
items.source_identity_basis: Opened WIPO Global Innovation Index 2026 official entry page and full GII 2026 results text released 29 September 2026. Checked the India economy profile/ranking results against the assigned country, and examined India’s official Economic Survey 2025–26 for separate investment-context evidence.
items.source_type: Intergovernmental composite innovation benchmark with national economic context
items.evidence_location: WIPO 2026 GII Results: middle-income economies and innovation-input/output performance; India country profile (2026 input rank 49, output rank 25); India Economic Survey 2025–26 sections 8.48–8.49 on gross R&D expenditure and business contribution.
items.specific_finding: India ranked 38th in the Global Innovation Index 2026, with innovation outputs 25th versus inputs 49th. WIPO describes sustained long-term innovation gains and an unusually strong position in ICT services exports. India’s Economic Survey independently reports R&D spending around 0.64% of GDP and a business-sector share around 41%, indicating that select high-performing output domains coexist with a relatively thin R&D resource base.
items.primary_evidence_summary: WIPO ranks India in the top 40 and as the leading economy in its income and regional groups; its output rank is much stronger than its input rank. India’s Economic Survey 2025–26 attributes low R&D spending intensity in part to the small private-sector contribution and details new RDI and research-foundation instruments aimed at raising capacity.
items.corroboration_assessment: The Indian Economic Survey provides separately produced national R&D spending and institutional-policy evidence, not an independent re-ranking of WIPO scores. The Government of India document corroborates constraints and the policy response, while WIPO supplies the international comparative index.
items.mechanism_and_ri_importance: India is an instructive case of the separation between aggregate research investment and specialised innovation outputs. European R&I comparisons should examine digital services, commercial linkages and innovation-finance mechanisms rather than assuming spending rank equals output rank.
items.eu_radar_comparison: No exact main Radar India 2026 GII entry was identified. This adds a structural input-output pattern and national funding context, not a claim that India exceeds EU economies in aggregate R&D performance.
items.method_and_limitations: GII rankings are composites and ordinal positions, not causal productivity measures. Indicators have different reference years (mostly 2024–26); the Indian Economic Survey’s R&D intensity series is older than GII publication and uses national definitions. Changes in rank also reflect changes in other countries.

items.primary_evidence_summary: WIPO’s multiyear composite benchmarking places South Africa among lower-income relative innovation overperformers. Its national science department separately reports 2024/25 GERD of R44.237bn in nominal terms, declining 1.9% after inflation and lower GERD/GDP intensity; the fall is concentrated in the business sector. These measurements describe different aspects of the system and are not intrinsically contradictory.
items.corroboration_assessment: The independently conducted South African National R&D Survey supplies financial data distinct from WIPO’s composite score; sectoral press coverage checks its reported values but relies on the same underlying survey. The two independent indicator systems support a nuanced structural insight, not a claim of independently audited WIPO rankings.
items.mechanism_and_ri_importance: A research system can remain productive relative to its income level while its business R&D base weakens in real terms. The contrast is consequential for innovation resilience, knowledge-transfer financing and international research partnerships involving South Africa.
items.eu_radar_comparison: No exact linked Radar entry was provided for South Africa’s WIPO profile. This adds evidence about African innovation strengths and financing constraints that can otherwise be missed by a Europe-first source selection.
items.method_and_limitations: Different reference periods: WIPO GII 2026 uses multiyear input data, while the latest South African survey reports financial year 2024/25. WIPO overperformance is relative to income and composite-method assumptions. Survey values are estimates; funding decline alone does not show reduced scientific output.
items.reviewer_notes: October 2026 South African survey is later than WIPO’s September release and is used as subsequent corroborating context, not to re-date the WIPO primary item.

items.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Singapore combines persistent high research investment, coordinated government priorities, translational programmes and targeted missions. items.reviewer_notes: WIPO findings are about structural strengths and conversion constraints rather than a new 2026 research breakthrough.

items.source_type: OECD comparative R&D statistical release
items.evidence_location: OECD 31 March 2026 release, sections “The United States and China reach the one-trillion-dollar R&D milestone in 2024”; “Understanding international comparisons ... purchasing power”; “R&D intensity ... China catches up”.
items.specific_finding: OECD estimates for 2024 indicate Chinese R&D expenditure was about 102% of US expenditure under the OECD’s contemporaneous purchasing-power conversion, but closer to 90–95% using a fixed 2020 PPP benchmark and about 50% at market exchange rates. China and the US are extraordinarily large research investors, yet asserting an unqualified Chinese R&D lead would overstate what the statistics show.
items.primary_evidence_summary: OECD estimates China’s 2024 GERD at roughly USD 0.86tr in 2020 PPP-adjusted dollars, marginally above the US under the OECD 2024 PPP ratio; both reach approximately USD 1tr when expressed in 2024 prices. The same OECD source explicitly demonstrates how different purchasing-power and exchange-rate conventions materially change the relative ranking.
items.corroboration_assessment: China’s 2024 national statistics independently publish the underlying RMB expenditure and R&D/GDP intensity; WIPO’s 2026 assessment uses a separate innovation-indicator methodology and reports China’s scale of research and technology clusters. However OECD’s Chinese monetary input relies on national reporting, so national figures and OECD conversions are not two independent audits.
items.mechanism_and_ri_importance: The sheer scale of Chinese research financing affects global equipment demand, scientific workforce competition, publication and patent ecosystems, industrial supply chains and collaborative opportunities. Exact PPP methods are crucial for realistic comparisons against US and EU technological capacity.
items.eu_radar_comparison: No exact corresponding main Radar link was supplied. This adds a global scale-and-methodology comparison that a Europe-centred monitoring process may miss; note the distinct finding on China’s R&D intensity and basic-research allocation under candidate 1.
items.method_and_limitations: R&D PPPs are based on GDP purchasing-power conversion, not R&D-specific prices; the result varies with benchmark year and exchange-rate approach. Input spending is not a direct measure of research quality, frontier capability or technological autonomy. OECD country inputs include self-reported statistics.
items.reviewer_notes: This finding is about scale and the methodological uncertainty of apparent China/US parity, not about Chinese research funding composition (candidate 1). Avoid stating flatly that China overtook the US.

items.source_identity_basis: Opened the OECD Main Science and Technology Indicators (MSTI) dataset landing page, explicitly identified as the OECD international R&D database. items.source_type: intergovernmental statistics / data-series landing page
items.evidence_location: OECD MSTI landing page: “MSTI release cycle and highlights”; accompanying 31 March 2026 OECD MSTI statistical release, section “R&D intensity in the OECD area remains unchanged, China catches up”. Chinese National Bureau of Statistics, 16 October 2026 communiqué, section I.
items.specific_finding: China’s reported R&D intensity reached approximately 2.7% of GDP in 2024, matching the OECD-area average and exceeding the EU’s roughly 2.1%; Chinese national data subsequently report 2.80% in 2025, with basic research accounting for 7.21% of R&D expenditure. This is a sustained change in research-system scale and mix, not a claim that China leads in all research quality or commercial outcomes.
items.primary_evidence_summary: The OECD MSTI database is a continuing statistical series and its 31 March 2026 release explicitly states that China had caught up with OECD-area R&D intensity in 2024, ahead of the EU ratio. China’s statistical agency separately publishes 2024 intensity of 2.69% and 2025 intensity of 2.80%, plus a 13.3% year-on-year increase in 2025 basic-research expenditure. The figures are internally consistent as a trajectory but have different reference years.
items.corroboration_assessment: The Chinese statistical communiqué on a different domain substantiates the 2024–25 intensity direction and breakdown; WIPO independently describes China’s broader innovation-output position using a different indicator system. OECD comparisons still rely partly on Chinese national returns and are not a field audit of claimed performance.
items.mechanism_and_ri_importance: An increasing share of national resources devoted to R&D, together with rising basic-research spending, changes the scale and composition of China’s research ecosystem. This merits comparison of talent pipelines, research quality, collaboration opportunities and strategic dependencies against European funding trends.
items.eu_radar_comparison: No exact main Radar entry was supplied for this source. This extends an EU-centred perspective by juxtaposing 2024 EU R&D intensity around 2.1% with the Chinese 2024 OECD estimate and later 2025 national reporting; topical overlap elsewhere in the archive cannot be ruled out.
items.method_and_limitations: OECD comparisons use reported national statistics and revised definitions; 2025 Chinese numbers are official self-reports, not independently audited outcomes. GDP denominators, preliminary releases and inflation adjustments matter; reported spending does not demonstrate research productivity or quality.
items.reviewer_notes: The assigned OECD page is a dataset portal, not a dated China article.
